issues.description: The problem statement and UML refer to a Meal class (described as 'Fully implemented') and all tasks use Meal as the type for orders and method parameters. However, the template repository does not provide an implemented Meal class (Meal.java is empty) and instead includes an Order class with the same structure/name semantics. This class-name/type mismatch (Meal vs Order) between the problem statement and the template will confuse students about which class to use/implement and may cause compile errors or duplicate implementations.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the template consistent with the problem statement: provide a fully implemented Meal class in the template (populate Meal.java) and remove or rename the provided Order class to avoid duplicate/ambiguous types. Alternatively, update the problem statement to use Order everywhere instead of Meal. Ensure the template Main.java references Meal (or is updated) so students work with the same type name as described in the specification.

issues.description: The problem statement and solution describe a core entity named 'Meal' (class Meal, with name and ingredients). The template repository instead provides an 'Order' class that models the same concept (it has name and ingredients). This mismatch (Meal vs Order) forces students to map the exercise requirements about Meal to a differently named class in the starter code, creating unnecessary cognitive overhead and potential confusion when tests and the final solution expect 'Meal'.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the identifier names so the same conceptual entity appears with a single name across artifacts. Rename the template's Order class/file to Meal (class Meal in Meal.java) and update any references in the template (e.g., Main comments) to use Meal, matching the problem statement and solution. Alternatively, add a Meal wrapper or alias that delegates to Order, but preferred fix is renaming Order -> Meal for consistency.
